messages.subject: Re: Factor scores from blavInspect()
messages.body_plain:
Hi!

In relation to this question about the relationship between applying lavPredict() and blavInspect() to a blavaan object, I was wondering whether the high correlations among the latent factor scores is also taken to be an indicator that the estimated factor scores by lavPredict() can be used for a blavaan object.

The reason I am asking is that unlike BlavPredict(), lavPredict() returns the labels of the latent factor scores, and so if multiple latent factors are estimated across multiple groups, then the data structure without the labels is a bit difficult to handle without a map of which order the latent factor scores are entered.

To compare: with two latent factors across two groups (where the groups correspond to a within-participant manipulation) and 769 participants, lavPredict() returns a list of 2 separated with labels across the two groups with a labelled column for each factor score with 769 rows. In contrast, BlavPredict() returns a list of 2 without labels with 16000 rows (for the different draws of the posterior distribution) with 3076 columns that are labelled "eta[1:1538, 1:2]".

I would assume that "eta[1:769, 1]" corresponds to the factor scores of the first latent factor in the first group, that "eta[1:769, 2]" corresponds to the second latent factor in the first group, that "eta[770:1538, 1]" corresponds to the first latent factor in the second group, and that "eta[770:1538, 2]" corresponds to the second latent factor in the second group. But without the labels of the factors and the groups (which here correspond to a within-participant manipulation), I would feel less confident assuming that this is the correct interpretation. And so, if I could just as well use the labelled factor scores returned by applying lavPredict() to the blavaan object, I would be more confident about which scores correspond to what.

Thanks in advance!

Best ,
Niels

messages.body_plain:
Hello Drs. Merkle and Garnier-Villarreal,

I hope this email finds you both well!

Thank you so much for the development and the phenomenal
updates to blavaan the last couple years, it has been an amazing package to
use!

I am working on a Monte Carlo simulation with Bayesian approximate
measurement invariance and had a couple of (hopefully) quick questions for you.

1.
I was looking for some documentation or
information the different variations of Stan that can be used as a ‘target = …”
in bcfa() (i.e., Stan, Stanclassic, and Stancond). Are the variations due to
the underlying code that blavaan creates to send to Stan? Would different
results be expected depending on which version is used? I have run some tests
and they seem to be very close (after setting the seed argument) but wanted to
double check.

2.
For Bayesian approximate measurement invariance
within blavaan, I saw the example code that Dr. Garnier-Villarreal posted (https://groups.google.com/g/blavaan/c/wBrkGIpgtlI/m/NGVddANZAwAJ),
which has been extremely helpful! Is the manual code (model excerpt below) analogous to using the wiggle argument? I ran some tests and had small
differences in WAIC and LOO using blavCompare() and the individual models had
results that matched (typically up to the third decimal place, but fairly
different PPP). I wasn't able to get the manual version to run in target = "stan", so some differences may be from that as well. I wanted to make sure that any of the results were not due to
the choice in which variation was used.

mod2_ap_stan <- '

Positive =~
prior(c("","normal(lambdaUNC[1,1,1],.01)"))*PosAFF1 +

prior(c("","normal(lambdaUNC[2,1,1],.01)"))*PosAFF2
+

prior(c("","normal(lambdaUNC[3,1,1],.01)"))*PosAFF3

Agency =~
prior(c("","normal(lambdaUNC[4,2,1],.01)"))*Agency1 +

prior(c("","normal(lambdaUNC[5,2,1],.01)"))*Agency2
+

prior(c("","normal(lambdaUNC[6,2,1],.01)"))*Agency3

Positive ~~ c(1, NA)*Positive

Agency ~~ c(1, NA)*Agency

            '

Thank you so very much for your time!

All the best,

-Eric

messages.body_plain:
Ye

As Ed mentioned, we need to write up a good example of these models for the website

Here is a quick example code, for three time points

#### Configural invariance model
configural <-'
verbal1 =~ item11 + item12 + item13
verbal2 =~ item21 + item22 + item23
verbal3 =~ item31 + item32 + item33
'
fitConfig <- bcfa(configural,
                  data=datsim,
                  std.lv <http://std.lv> = TRUE,
                n.chains = 3,
                burnin=3000,
                sample=2000
             )

### Weak invariance ###
weak <-'
verbal1 =~ L11*item11 + L12*item12 + L13*item13
verbal2 =~ L11*item21 + L12*item22 + L13*item23
verbal3 =~ L11*item31 + L12*item32 + L13*item33

verbal1 ~~ 1*verbal1
verbal2 ~~ NA*verbal2
verbal3 ~~ NA*verbal3
'
fitWeak <- bcfa(weak,
                  data=datsim,
                  std.lv <http://std.lv> = TRUE,
                  n.chains = 3,
                  burnin=2000,
                  sample=2000
                )

##### Strong Invariance #################
strong <-'
verbal1 =~ L11*item11 + L12*item12 + L13*item13
verbal2 =~ L11*item21 + L12*item22 + L13*item23
verbal3 =~ L11*item31 + L12*item32 + L13*item33

##Latent variances
verbal1 ~~ 1*verbal1
verbal2 ~~ NA*verbal2
verbal3 ~~ NA*verbal3

## Intercepts

item11 ~ I11*1
item21 ~ I21*1
item31 ~ I31*1
